fig1_intensive_invariance.svg: The same rescaling that sends every extensive property up the diagonal (module 1.3) leaves the intensive ones untouched. Copying a 2 kg, 1.6 m$^3$ system $k$ times multiplies mass and volume by $k$, but density $\rho=m/V$ and specific volume $v=V/m$ (density, specific_volume) stay pinned at their original value — the ratio of two extensive quantities cancels the extent. is_size_independent confirms it for an eight-fold scale-up. Temperature and pressure behave the same way, which is why they can be quoted for a substance without saying how much of it you have.
fig2_mass_average.svg: Intensive properties add over subsystems only when weighted by mass. Two parcels of the same substance at 300 K and 500 K are combined while the mass split is swept: the correct mixture temperature (mass_average) runs linearly from 500 K to 300 K, while the unweighted mean of the two values is stuck at 400 K. They coincide at exactly one point, the 50/50 split. Averaging intensive properties without their masses is one of the most common bookkeeping errors in mixture problems.
